lecture.title: Python Basics
lecture.say: Welcome. This chapter is the prompt, the values it computes with, the operators that combine them, the names that remember them, and a first program. Every code slide shows the code, a plain explanation, and what the run printed as a table, chart or drawing.

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: Four parts: values and types, operations, names and functions, and a first program. Each range is a run of slides you can jump to. The chapter-code tab of the page holds the same examples in the same order.

lecture.title: Three questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: Three questions to carry through the chapter. Which operations can raise an error, and which? Which results can surprise a student? And what has changed in current Python since the book?

lecture.title: Part 1: Values and types
lecture.say: Part one. The shell evaluates an expression and prints its value. Every value has a data type: integer, float or string. Notice which results surprise you.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: values and types
lecture.say: A calculator with a screen is the shell. An expression is a recipe line that ends in one value. A data type is the label on a container. Ask students to add their own everyday picture.

lecture.title: The shell: type an expression, get a value
lecture.say: The shell is a calculator that answers. In a program you write print yourself. Ask students to predict 2 + 3 * 6 before the run, and why it is not 30.

lecture.title: Story: a Christmas hobby named after a comedy troupe
lecture.say: Guido van Rossum began Python in the Christmas week of 1989 at CWI in Amsterdam. The name comes from Monty Python. Ask students which of today's examples they would have written in a language without this readability.

lecture.title: Data types: int, float and str
lecture.say: Type names the data type of any value. A whole number plus a float gives a float. Ask: what type does 7 + 1.0 have, and why?

lecture.title: Integers never overflow
lecture.say: Python integers never overflow. 2 to the power 100 has 31 digits and is exact. Int turns text into a number, and cuts a float without rounding.

lecture.title: Floats are honest about being approximate
lecture.say: Zero point one plus zero point two is not exactly zero point three. Floats are binary fractions, so many decimals do not fit. Division with a slash always gives a float.

lecture.title: Strings: text between quotes
lecture.say: A string is text between quotes. Len counts characters. The text seven and the number seven are different values; Python never converts between them silently.

lecture.title: Part 2: Operations
lecture.say: Part two. Operators combine values. Precedence decides who goes first, and parentheses override it. Plus and star also work on strings, with a different meaning.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: operators
lecture.say: Operators are verbs between values. Precedence is the order of work: chop before you stir. Go through the eight pictures and ask which one students remember best.

lecture.title: Seven operators for numbers
lecture.say: Seven operators: plus, minus, times, divide, floor divide, remainder, power. The slash always gives a float. The double slash and the percent sign work as a pair.

lecture.title: Who goes first: operator precedence
lecture.say: The power goes first, then times and divide, then plus and minus. Parentheses override. Minus three to the power two is minus nine, because the power binds tighter. Predict, then run.

lecture.title: Division three ways: quotient and remainder
lecture.say: Twenty-three candies in boxes of seven: three boxes and two left. Floor division gives the boxes, percent gives the rest. Floor division rounds down, so minus seven by two is minus four.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: operations on text
lecture.say: Concatenation glues strips of text, replication photocopies them. Str is the label maker that turns any value into text. Keep the pictures; the code comes next.

lecture.title: String concatenation: + joins text
lecture.say: Plus joins strings and adds no space. Joining text to a number is a TypeError, because Python does not convert silently. Str fixes it. Errors are answers: read the message.

lecture.title: String replication: * repeats text
lecture.say: Star repeats a string. The count must be a whole number; a float raises a TypeError. Zero copies give the empty string. The chart shows how long each result is.

lecture.title: Part 3: Names and functions
lecture.say: Part three. A variable is a name for a value. Print shows, input reads, and str, int, float and len convert and measure. Errors are answers too.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: names
lecture.say: A variable is a labelled jar. Print is the loudspeaker, input is the suggestion box. Everything in the box is paper, so even a number arrives as text.

lecture.title: Variables: names that remember
lecture.say: An assignment gives a name to a value. Assign again and the name refers to a new value. Names are case-sensitive: Spam was never assigned, so Python raises a NameError.

lecture.title: print: the function that shows
lecture.say: Print takes any number of items. The options sep and end change the separator and the ending. Print with nothing in the parentheses writes an empty line.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: functions and modules
lecture.say: Len is a ruler for text. Int and float are machines with a slot in and a slot out. Ask which machine rejects the input and why.

lecture.title: Conversions and len: built-in functions
lecture.say: Str, int and float convert. Len counts characters; a number has no length, so convert it to text first. The table shows input, function, result and type.

lecture.title: Errors are answers too
lecture.say: A ValueError means the type is right but the content is wrong. A TypeError means the type itself does not fit the operation. Reading the error name tells you where to look.

lecture.title: input always returns text
lecture.say: Input always returns text, even when the person types a number. Plus on text glues, plus on numbers adds. Convert with int before you calculate.

lecture.title: Modules: import opens a toolbox
lecture.say: Import brings in a toolbox. The dot reaches inside it for a function, sqrt, or a value, pi. Standard library modules are free and always installed.

lecture.title: Part 4: A first program
lecture.say: Part four. A first program uses everything so far. Then we take it apart line by line, and finish with the binary digits behind every number.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: a program and its bits
lecture.say: A program is a recipe. Dissecting it is taking a clock apart. Binary is a row of light switches. Each picture comes back on the slide that follows.

lecture.title: Story: where hello, world began, in 1972
lecture.say: The first hello, world was in a 1972 tutorial for the language B. In B the text needed three variables; in Python it is one line. Ask what a first program proves: that writing, running and seeing output all work.

lecture.title: Your first program
lecture.say: The first program greets, asks, measures and calculates. Because the page has no keyboard, the example names the text input would return. Trace it line by line in the table.

lecture.title: Dissecting the program: join or fill in
lecture.say: Two ways to build the same sentence: join five pieces with plus and str, or fill slots in an f-string. The f-string is shorter and needs no str. Which would you rather read?

lecture.title: Story: Leibniz wrote every number with only 0 and 1
lecture.say: Leibniz described binary arithmetic in 1679 and in a paper for the Paris Academy in 1703. Bouvet's letter from Peking showed the I Ching hexagrams as binary numbers. Ask: why do computers prefer two digits?

lecture.title: How computers store numbers: binary
lecture.say: Bin shows binary digits, int with base 2 reads them. Eight binary digits make a byte and hold 256 values. Each place is a power of two; the chart shows which places are on for the number five.

lecture.title: Current Python adds more
lecture.say: Python moves on. The shell and its error messages improved in 3.13. The free-threaded build is experimental. F-strings have a formal grammar. Check each row against its source.

lecture.title: Summary
lecture.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart counts the code examples of each part. Everything is on the chapter page, in the same order.

lecture.title: Practice Questions

stories.title: A Christmas hobby named after a comedy troupe
stories.who: Guido van Rossum, a programmer at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica (CWI)
stories.where: At CWI in Amsterdam; the source code was posted to the alt.sources Usenet group
stories.story: In the Christmas week of December 1989 the office at CWI in Amsterdam was closed, and Guido van Rossum, who worked there on the Amoeba project, started a hobby scripting language, a descendant of ABC, that would be easier to read than shell scripts. He named it after the British comedy troupe Monty Python, not after the snake. He posted version 0.9.0 to the alt.sources newsgroup in February 1991. Every prompt on these slides runs the grown-up descendant of that hobby.
stories.lesson: The tool you are learning began as a one-week hobby
stories.source: Wikipedia, 'Guido van Rossum' and the history of Python (project begun December 1989 at CWI, name from Monty Python, 0.9.0 posted to alt.sources in February 1991), opened 2026-10-25. Photo: Daniel Stroud, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

stories.title: Where hello, world began, in 1972
stories.who: Brian Kernighan, a researcher at Bell Laboratories
stories.where: Bell Laboratories; page 6 of The C Programming Language (Prentice Hall, 1978)
stories.story: In 1972 Brian Kernighan, at Bell Laboratories, wrote the first known program that puts the words hello and world together, as a teaching example in 'A Tutorial Introduction to the Language B'. A beginner needs a first program that does one visible thing: print a greeting. The language B held only four characters per constant, so the text had to sit in three variables. The 1978 book 'The C Programming Language' by Kernighan and Ritchie made the greeting famous. In Python the same program is one line.
stories.lesson: A first program proves that write, run and see all work
stories.source: Wikipedia, '"Hello, World!" program' (Kernighan, 'A Tutorial Introduction to the Language B', Bell Laboratories, 1972; Kernighan and Ritchie, 'The C Programming Language', Prentice Hall, 1978, page 6), opened 2026-10-25. Photo: Ben Lowe, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.

stories.title: Leibniz wrote every number with only 0 and 1
stories.when: 15 March 1679; letter of 1703; paper printed in 1705
stories.who: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, philosopher and mathematician, and the Jesuit Joachim Bouvet
stories.where: The paper went to the Academie Royale des Sciences in Paris; Bouvet's letter came from Peking
stories.story: Leibniz first noted binary arithmetic on 15 March 1679: every number written with the two digits 0 and 1. On 1 April 1703 a letter from the Jesuit Joachim Bouvet in Peking reached him and showed that the hexagrams of the Chinese I Ching are binary numbers. Leibniz saw order in them and printed his paper 'Explication de l'arithmetique binaire' in 1705. Every number is a sum of powers of two: 5 is 4 plus 1, written 101. Computers store numbers this way.
stories.lesson: Every number is a sum of powers of two

ndiag.title: How the interpreter evaluates an expression
ndiag.read_from: chapter 1, Entering Expressions into the Interactive Shell: Expression (a piece of code that evaluates to a value, built from literals, names, operators and function calls), Operator (the symbol between its operands; the type of the operands decides its meaning), Precedence (** first, then *, /, //, %, then + and -; parentheses override it)
ndiag.why: the explanations describe what Python does with an expression in order - read it, decide which operator applies first, apply it, repeat until one value is left - with the type of the operands deciding the meaning on the way: a workflow
